Hello, I was using a [product_name] with article number [article_no] and firmware version [version_no]. After I created and uploaded a new project, the device stopped working. Now, upon powering up, the screen is completely blank. If I press and hold the 'esc' key, I briefly see 'detecting...' for a few seconds before the screen turns off. The device also isn’t visible in [product_name] software. Is there a way to recover it?

I haven’t come across this exact problem before. What do you mean by 'blank screen' after switching on—does it mean absolutely nothing is displayed? Are you able to access the system menu of [product_name] at all?

The screen stays blank as soon as the device is powered up, with no display and no backlight. I cannot access any menus because nothing is visible. Only when pressing the ESC key, a 'detecting...' message appears for a few seconds. The LAN LED blinks more quickly if a cable is connected, and occasionally even when disconnected.

How did you transfer the program—was it via network cable or SD card? If you used an SD card, please check if any pins are bent and try to start the device without the SD card. If you used the network cable, try pinging the device; if it does not respond, it may be faulty. At that point, you may need to replace it.

Based on your description, it seems the [product_name] is defective. You should consider creating a support request.

I also believe the [product_name] is faulty. You will need to replace it.

Hello everyone, I'm new to programming [product_name] or any other PLC, so please be patient with me. I'm trying to set up a pushbutton (using a pulse pushbutton) to start a contactor. Is it possible to use the same pushbutton (by pressing it again) to reset the contactor? I assume this would involve a latching relay or a similar mechanism, but I want to avoid issues in case the pushbutton is accidentally held down, causing the contactor to repeatedly turn on and off. Any advice or tips would be greatly appreciated. Thanks in advance.

Normally, a pulse logic relay needs two signals at its input to change state (on-off). Even a latch relay requires a reset input to return to the on state. So, if your pushbutton remains in contact, it's typically not an issue. However, if you want to avoid concerns, you could use a timer (delay on), which will reset the logic after a few seconds.

Hi [user_name], it appears your setup is functioning as intended. Thank you for your assistance. Best regards.

Can someone assist me? My [product_name] display only shows three menu options: Setup, Network, and Diagnostics. I'm unsure how to perform a factory reset. Any support would be appreciated. Thank you.

Try checking the IP settings or your Ethernet cable. You can also start 'cmd' and use the 'ping' command for the device IP.

A factory reset can only be done with [product_name] [version_no] FS04. For the [product_name] [article_no] Standard, this feature is not available. The limited menu appears when the device is set to operator mode. To access administrator mode, you'll need to enter the password. Attached is an extract from [document] detailing the procedure.

Appreciate the assistance.

Thank you!

The relationship between air pressure and output voltage of the sensor is: Voltage = 10 (Pressure - 5.5). Attached is the corresponding graph. How can I calculate pressure based on the voltage input? I understand that [product_name] can handle linear formulas using the 'Gain' and 'Offset' in the 'Analog Amplifier' block, but what about sensors like this? Thanks for your help.

Hello [user_name], Hello [user_name], Previously: [product_name] does not excel at complex calculations; it only uses fixed point arithmetic (16 bit integer), with no floating point support. In my view, the only viable approach is dividing the curve into several straight-line segments for processing. I valued the input from [user_name] regarding this topic, especially their post about CO2 calculations and implementing mathematical equations with [product_name] on 7/17/2009. [document]

For your second question, you need a 24 VDC power supply to connect to the analog output module, ensuring it works with your 230V system. You may find additional details here: [url]

Hello [user_name], If you only have three phases (L1, L2, and L3) and no neutral (N), is it possible to power on a [product_name] 230RC and DM8 module using just two phases (L1 and L2, with L2 as the reference)? Thanks!

You can connect the inputs of a 230V [product_name] or its 230V extension modules to different phases, but you need to group them in sets of four inputs. Please see the attached excerpt from the manual for more details.

Hello, Based on your description, it sounds like you have a three-phase power supply without neutral. If the voltage between the two phases is less than 254V AC, the 230V [product_name] might work since its maximum supported voltage is 254V AC. However, this is not guaranteed. Hope this helps.

Hi [user_name], Thank you for your help. The schematic displays the power lines and input ports. Is there anything I might be missing or not understanding? Best regards, [user_name]

You can use a different phase instead of neutral as the power reference. Use L1 and L2, L1 and L3, or L2 and L3 to supply power. If you also want to use the remaining phase for inputs, they can only be assigned within the prescribed groups of four. Once you use a phase for the 'N' terminal in the power supply, you cannot assign it to the input signals.

Hi [user_name], I'm not saying you're wrong, but how does this actually work? If two phases from a three-phase network are connected, doesn't that mean the unit receives 400VAC? In a three-phase setup, voltage between a neutral and one phase equals 230VAC, while between two phases it's 400VAC. Is a [product_name] designed to handle such voltage?

It depends on the specific three-phase system. If it's a 3-phase 400VAC network, your concern is valid. However, some networks use 3-phase 230VAC. Your point is important: this only applies to a three-phase 230VAC network.

The issue arises because [user_name] did not provide complete specifications. In some regions, like Germany, a standard three-phase system uses 3~/N/PE/AC400V/50Hz, while other countries or certain companies may use different setups, such as 3~/PE/AC480V/60Hz with a separate control voltage of 1~/N/PE/AC240V/60Hz. [user_name] needs to verify the voltage between two phases before connecting it to the [product_name] controller to prevent damage. Refer to the operating instructions for the module's supported voltage range. Regards, [user_name]

Why is the panel's clock running 6 minutes and 16 seconds late compared to the actual time, as referenced by a DCF77 clock? Entering an NTP IP address in the settings does not correct the issue. Is this something that cannot be fixed, or is there an alternative solution?

You can synchronize the time between different controller versions and an operator panel. In the NTP settings of the controller, set it up as an NTP client and provide the IP address of an NTP server. This will allow the device to obtain the correct time and date. Within your engineering environment, set up a connection for the operator panel using the relevant communication driver. This makes it possible to activate area pointers for synchronization purposes. To synchronize time, make sure the global area pointer for date and time is enabled for the connection using the correct communication driver. Specify address VW991 for this configuration.

Initially, synchronization didn't work. Eventually, I located the issue: in the Connections -> Parameter section, the IP address for the station was incorrect. After correcting it, the clock displayed the correct time. Thanks for the assistance.

Does anyone know the maximum load of the [product_name] analog output at 0-10V configuration? Some specifications mention a minimum load of 5kOhm, with a maximum of around 2mA (at 12V). This may be insufficient for certain inputs. If the current limit is 2mA, does anyone know of a driver to amplify the 0-10V analog output? Any advice would be appreciated.

For instance, I need to operate an RGBW LED dimmer that has a 0-10V input lower than 5kOhm. Currently, our temporary and costly solution involves using an external KFD11JVTN amplifier from sb-controls.

Hello, I am working on a project extension. The original setup uses a [product_name] as the main controller. The new machinery requires extra I/O, and is located far from the main panel. Instead of installing extensive cabling, I considered adding a local [product_name] at the new machine and connecting it to the main one, essentially using it as remote I/O. Previously, when more I/O than a single [product_name] and its expansions could manage was needed, I implemented a Master to Master connection, with the main controller running the main program and the second controller managing its own I/O mapping. This approach succeeded, though I now wonder if a Master/Slave configuration might have been preferable. I'm uncertain whether to pursue a Master/Master or a Master/Slave design for this expansion. A Master/Slave setup offers a single program in one location, with the second controller acting as remote I/O. Conversely, Master/Master offers more flexibility for testing and simulating inputs, as one can simulate inputs on either controller independently. Are there other pros or cons to either arrangement, or am I missing anything?

Your reasoning is sound. The best choice depends on your project's requirements. Everyone has to determine for themselves whether a master/master or master/slave structure will suit their needs.

Hi [user_name], keep in mind that a master/master connection provides double the number of inputs/outputs and available memory, which you don't get with master/slave. In master/slave mode, the slave only acts as a decentralized expansion module. Regards, [user_name]

Are you certain about that? In a master/slave configuration, the master is capable of accessing all digital inputs and controlling all digital outputs on the slave device.

Hello! I have a question regarding the [product_name] module intended for PT100 temperature measurement. I am considering using it to monitor the temperature of a power generator. I haven't purchased the PT100 module yet and would like to know if I still need to connect a temperature sensor to it, or does the module function as a sensor itself? Also, where should I install the module to accurately measure the generator's temperature? Any advice would be appreciated. Thank you!

Yes, you need to buy a PT100 sensor. The module is designed for direct connection with a sensor. For best results, place the sensor in the return line from the engine 'head' to the radiator. Additionally, it's advisable to use a flow or level sensor at the water reservoir. This setup lets you read the temperature, and if there is belt failure or water loss, it helps protect the engine.

Thank you for the information. I'd like to mention that I'm using a 5KVA generator for home use, which doesn't have a radiator system. Could you advise on which battery voltage sensors are compatible with [product_name]? I want to measure the battery voltage used to start the generator. Also, could you share the price of the AM2 PT100 module? If I'm using the 12/24 V version with 4 analog inputs, is it possible to connect a temperature sensor to any of these inputs?

First, please avoid posting the same question multiple times so that moderators can manage the forums efficiently. Now to your questions: If your engine is air-cooled, you may not need a PT100 sensor unless you plan to display temperature data. You could consider thermostats that fit into the cylinder head and provide a NO/NC contact, which can then be connected to [product_name] (similar to those used in small transformers or welding equipment). You can find such products online, e.g. [url]. For measuring battery voltage, you'll need a converter from 12 or 24 V DC to 0–10 V, such as those described at [url] (refer to 'interface technology', page 1–37). There are other solutions too, like battery chargers with auxiliary contacts: [url]. The AM PT100 module is typically around 100 Euros, but using a PT100 to 0–10 V converter is less expensive if you have an analog input available. Best of luck.

Sorry for reposting the same question; I just wanted to reach more people who might have insights. Your help has been very valuable. There are four analog inputs available – I can connect a battery voltage sensor to one of them, but I'm unsure about PT100 integration. Why is there a separate module for PT100 sensors instead of connecting them directly to an analog input? Can I use a PT100 with one of the existing analog inputs just to display the machine's temperature, without needing the dedicated PT100 module? I'm working on a cost-sensitive project involving ATS, AMF, temperature, and battery voltage sensors with [product_name] 12/24 version. Thank you for your continued support, and apologies for my earlier mistake.

If I connect thermostats to the engine cylinder and interface them with [product_name], will their status be displayed as temperature readings? By using thermostats, do I still need the AM PT100 module, or can I connect them directly to the analog input?

If you have a PT100 sensor, there are two ways to connect it to [product_name]: (a) use the dedicated PT100 module; (b) use a PT100-to-0–10 V converter. Both options allow temperature readings from the analog input, letting you display or monitor the values. If you use a bimetallic or contact-type thermostat, you'll connect it via a digital input. In this case, you can only detect on/off states, not actual temperature values.

Hi, Certain blocks are not permitted within a UDF, including I and Q. Essentially, a UDF operates similarly to other special functions; I and Q must be connected only at the block's inputs and outputs and are not allowed within a UDF itself. Additionally, you cannot include message text within a UDF. If you attempt to use restricted blocks when creating a UDF from existing code, the system delivers a clear warning message. I hope this clarifies things.

I've attached a drawing showing my setup, but this example uses 24V from the power supply instead of battery voltage.

Using just a resistor on a current loop input for the AM2 module is not advisable. Instead, use two resistors to lower the voltage (maximum 10V), then measure with the 0–10V input on the AM2 module. For example, connect a 5.6k Ohm and a 1k Ohm resistor in series and measure across the 1k resistor; you'll get roughly one-sixth of the input voltage—56V would result in about 8.5V at the input. If you have the correct [product_name] base module (the full DC variant), you might be able to use its analog inputs directly and skip the AM2 module.

You could consider a current transformer that's available in suitable ratios, then use a resistor for finer adjustment. Connect the output to an interface board that converts current to voltage. These boards are inexpensive online and allow you to tweak zero and span, so you could connect the analog input on the [product_name] base module without needing the AM2 module.

Are current transformer modules available for DC measurements?

Yes, DC current sensing modules are available. Some output 5V, and there may be 10V models too—contact the seller for confirmation. See example products on [url].

Here's another example of a DC current transducer module: [url]

Why convert voltage to current, then back using a current transducer, and let the [product_name] input module convert it again using its internal resistor? Just use two resistors as described, and connect directly to the analog input on the base module.

I agree—using only resistors is best, with 5.6k and 1k values recommended. At 56V, you'll reach about 10.1V, but if your charger supports equalizing it could go up to 60V. Keep it simple; with 1W resistors the current remains safe around 7mA.

Choose resistor values as needed, but remember the analog input's internal resistance introduces a load resistor in your voltage divider design. You can adjust scaling in the [product_name] to account for resistor tolerances and the internal resistance.

In a two-resistor setup, be sure to connect the battery's negative terminal to the correct point on the [product_name] power supply. Resistor calculations should also factor in tolerance and the internal resistance of the module. Calibration within the [product_name] software can help refine your measurement.

I've updated my original drawing to correct a small error regarding potential. The [product_name] pin M must connect to potential M—otherwise, the common ground has no purpose.

I prefer current measurement because it protects against overvoltage. If a resistor is bypassed by accident, it could put 24V straight onto the 0-10V ADC input.

Analog inputs on the base module can also serve as digital inputs with DC24V (max DC28.8V), so up to this voltage there’s no risk. Alternatively, you can use a Zener diode parallel to the resistor to limit voltage, for example, to DC12V.

There’s only a single VM memory, byte-addressed. User addressable range is V0.0 to V850.7, a total of 6808 bits or 851 bytes. VM memory bytes are VB0 to VB850. For instance, Word 0 in VM memory (VW0) contains 2 bytes: VB0 and VB1, with VB0 holding bits V0.0 to V0.7 and VB1 holding V1.0 to V1.7. If you’re using VW0 for a timer, you can’t use V0.0 to V1.7 for other functions such as starting the timer.

When the EN input on the Data Log module detects a rising edge from 0 to 1, a new row is added. If EN stays high, further changes are not logged until the next qualifying edge. There must be a minimum gap of 500 ms between edge changes for subsequent data to be recorded.

How are you controlling the EN input in your code? It's possible that logging is not occurring properly. If events intended to trigger logging are switched in parallel, the required 500 ms interval between triggers may not be maintained.

The inputs shown occur at different times unless a specific input is already active. This is for a gate system with inputs for up/down commands, limit switches, and safety signals. Some inputs might happen within 500ms, but not consistently. There should be multiple rows with I2 or I8 being high, but those entries are missing.

Therefore, it's uncertain whether: (a) the 500 ms pause between events is maintained, and (b) fewer than two inputs are active at the same time. If one input is already on and others arrive at overlapping times, those events are not logged.

I am wondering if it is possible to have active voltage on the input side when the device loses power, or if this could cause hardware damage. I need this information for both 12/24 Vdc and 230 Vac systems.

Could you provide more details?

If the power fails, there will be no active voltage present.

That's not always correct. There can be a power failure only for the [product_name] and/or the expansion modules, while the peripherals remain powered. The wiring and protection setup are unclear here—the original poster should clarify.

If you're referring to just the [product_name] or its expansion modules losing power, but the connected peripherals still being powered, then there should be no issue.

Yes, that's the case for my setup. I have a [product_name] powered by a 230V supply with its own switch, referred to as 'SERVICES'. There are inputs coming from a separate 230V supply dedicated to lighting, called 'LIGHTS', each with their own protection. Both originate from the main supply, so they're only connected when both switches are on. If SERVICES is off but LIGHTS is on, some inputs to the [product_name] remain active while the device itself is off. Is this safe? The same scenario could happen with a 24Vdc system, if the input and device power lines are switched separately. You might get active inputs while the device power is off. Is it also safe to use analog instead of digital inputs in such cases? Best Regards, [user_name]

Hello, Be cautious with 230V lines—SERVICE and LIGHT may be supplied by different phases. As long as inputs within a group use the same phase, it's fine. If different phases are mixed within one input group, you must separate them; otherwise, hardware damage may occur. A [product_name] has two input groups: I1–I4 and I5–I8. Don't connect different phases to inputs within the same group. For a third phase, you'd need a suitable expansion module ([product_name]). Refer to the wiring diagram in the [document] for correct setup. Hope this helps.

I'm referring to a single-phase circuit. Specifically, there is a power switch that can shut off the supply to the [product_name], while input power remains active. Is it safe to have active input channels in this circuit when the device power is switched off?

Is it possible and safe to connect 12/24V AC/DC to one relay output and 230V AC to another on a [product_name] base module with 230V supply? The specifications mention 4 relay outputs with a maximum load of 10A.

It is safe as long as the current remains below 10A. As a precaution, it's common practice to use an additional relay to protect the controller outputs from potential damage, especially if something goes wrong with the 230V connection.

To address the question directly: Yes, you can connect 12/24V AC/DC to one relay output and 230V AC to another on a [product_name] base module. The relay terminals are potential-free, meaning they aren't joined internally or to any common potential. The manual's note—'Relay rated voltage 240 VAC/VDC'—refers only to the maximum allowable voltage.

That matches my understanding. I wanted to confirm because in other home automation modules I've used, similar specifications came with warnings against mixing low safety voltages (12V) with higher standard ones (230V) due to the components being close together, which could cause arcing in case of failure. Their certifications require these warnings, so mixing voltages or phases in the same module is not permitted, even though it might work. I wanted to check if [product_name] has a similar safety restriction, or if its construction avoids these issues.

Voltages are not mixed internally. As mentioned, the relay contacts are potential-free, and the insulation distance between terminals is sufficient for 230V. Preventing wiring mistakes that could mix voltages is the responsibility of the installer.

Summing up: it is safe to connect an 8VAC bell to one output and, for example, 230V lights to another output—connections are sufficiently separated both inside and outside the module.

The [product_name] can still operate, but you should be aware that the wiring for the 24VDC supply and connections on the [product_name] are not isolated from earth and 0V. With a plug, you can't be certain about the configuration of line and neutral.

Hello, I'm new to [product_name] and have a challenge in calculating meters on a plastic film line. My setup uses a roller with a 60mm diameter and one proximity sensor, which generates one pulse for every 188.5mm of roller movement. The speed of the line is about 20m/min. 1000mm can't be measured exactly, because 1000mm isn't a precise multiple of 188.5mm. The display may show exactly 1000mm, but this isn't the true measured length. With 1834mm divided by 11, you get 166.73mm per pulse—but your setup actually gives 60mm x Pi = 188.5mm per pulse. You can't freely choose these values if you want displayed and actual lengths to match. Regards, [user_name]

Hi [user_name], the short answer is that the AM2 expansion module cannot be used as a HART module. It operates only as an analog module. For more details, refer to the technical data: [url]. HART communication requires specific electronics, including a modem, which the AM2 does not have. For information on HART modules, see this Texas Instruments document: [url]. HART signals are superimposed FSK signals over 4-20mA analog messages ([url]). The AM2 simply reads analog input values and cannot interpret HART data. There are no HART-capable modules in the [product_name] offerings. If you need to process HART signals, consider a different platform, such as ET 200M or ET 200SP: • ET 200M HART analog input: [url] • ET 200SP HART analog input: [url]. Hope this helps. Also, as another user mentioned, if you only wish to read the analog signal and not HART variables, the AM2 module will work for analog measurement. Apologies for any confusion. D.C.

HART protocol combines digital communication with an analog signal. From your description, you seem interested only in reading the 4-20mA analog value, not the digital portion. In this case, yes—the AM2 module can be used to read just the analog component. By design, the HART signal does not affect the analog measurement. For further information, see this discussion: [document]. Remember, your field device may require configuration via HART, which you might need to do using either a built-in interface or a handheld programmer. Be sure no control functions like PID are active in the instrument. Please consult your E+H supplier.

If you need to collect data from remote locations via NB-IOT or GPRS, perhaps once an hour, Modbus can be more efficient as the native protocol is quite 'chatty' (with traffic between 3 and 30 kbit/sec depending on the number of data points, and traffic remains constant). For my needs, it's not ideal.

Depending on your application, it can make sense to favor Modbus due to the continuous traffic of the native protocol. [user_name], have you verified that your server device was fully set up as a Modbus server and is continuously providing data?

The main concern isn't protocol 'chattiness,' but the issue where, after a certain period, all data resets to zero.

Try customizing the polling interval for Modbus queries from your client device. By default, [product_name] polls Modbus registers every 80 milliseconds—which is more frequent than necessary. Setting it to around 500 milliseconds or even longer may be sufficient for most tasks. Frequent polling may occasionally cause unexpected issues.

By default, there is no active polling interval set—the time values are inaccessible and greyed out in the settings.

The default polling rate is at its maximum, with approximately 10 to 12 queries each second.

You'll notice this when mapping parameters and seeing the use of VD instead of VW. There might be a workaround for assigning larger values, but I haven't found one. Modbus devices can often export values in multiple formats. Look for alternative registers with float or double output—in such cases, you can use a float-to-integer converter and display larger values with parameters like eAq. Keep in mind, though, that you can't perform calculations using long integer or float types, nor compare such values directly.

Thanks. Could you clarify the purpose of the Analog amplifier block? Why not simply connect Network Analog Input to an Analog Flag?

If you wish to display any analog value, you'll need to use an analog block for selecting a display parameter. You can also use other analog blocks, like the analog threshold trigger. The analog amplifier block should follow at least an analog flag, and the threshold trigger should be followed by an open connector—since you can't leave an output unconnected. Using an analog block also allows you to set a decimal point for representing units correctly, such as showing 327.67 from a value of 32767 for kilowatt-hours.

Hello everyone, The [product_name]-[article_no] introduces several new function blocks. In this review, I'd like to discuss the "analog filter" block from an application-oriented perspective: The "analog filter" block computes a sliding average based on n previous values over time. Achieving this in hardware typically requires significant effort, so my previously published circuits were limited to n = 4, 8, or 10. The block's capability to handle up to 256 values, as noted in the documentation, is impressive. However, the permitted n values are restricted to a few predefined options (it would be far more useful if users could freely select any value between 1 and 256, with referencing and external triggering also supported). I have concerns about how the time interval between sampled values is specified—it is strictly linked to the (variable) cycle frequency of [product_name], which is essentially the program frequency. As per documentation: “[product_name] processes analog values every cycle. The number of cycles matches the configured sampling count.” Since the cycle frequency changes, this implementation only ensures the filter is suitable for analog values from blocks updated each cycle, not directly from analog inputs. Sampling intervals for analog input values should be defined by their own sampling rates, with user-adjustable update frequencies (typically every 50 ms or 300 ms, or a multiple thereof). Otherwise, incorrect results may occur depending on real signal characteristics. Summary: The "analog filter" block unfortunately cannot reliably filter analog input signals, because its operation is based on [product_name]’s cycle frequency, which diverges from the actual input sampling rates (e.g., 300 ms for basic modules, 50 ms for expansion modules). This can cause significant differences between the filtered outputs and true signal values. Since external triggering for sampling times isn’t available, the block generally falls short for accurate moving average calculations in most use cases. Best regards [user_name]

It's really a matter of personal preference and each user should choose what fits their needs. Diagram mode is generally intended for programs that run on just one [product_name] and don't require interaction with other devices. Network project mode is best suited when your [product_name] needs to communicate with multiple devices, like other controllers, operator panels, or compatible systems.

For standalone programming, use the diagram mode (.lsc file format). The network project mode (.mnp) doesn’t provide extra value for single-device setups. Even with diagram mode, you can still connect to other devices (another controller, interface device, Modbus, or compatible systems) via the network connections menu. The software remembers and automatically opens the most recent diagram files, while network project files need to be opened manually. An advantage of network project mode is that you can search for compatible devices on the network—for example, if you are unsure of the device IP address. Otherwise, network mode can take up more screen space without additional benefits for simple setups.

In my experience, network mode makes it much easier to connect multiple devices together. Setting up connections between several controllers is straightforward in network mode compared to diagram mode, where it can be more involved.

Hello, I'm trying to create a block using mathematical instructions to process the analog input module, which ranges from 0 to 100 and divides it by 100. However, if the input is in the range 0-49, the output should be 0, and if it's 50-100, the output should be 1. Is it possible for the result to be 0.6 when the input is 60?

The controller performs internal calculations using floating-point arithmetic, but externally it only provides values as fixed-point numbers. The result always shows at least one decimal place, rounded accordingly: values below 0.5 are rounded down, and values of 0.5 or above are rounded up.

Keep in mind that the analog outputs internally in the controller use values from 0 to 1000. Here, 0 corresponds to 0 Volt or 0 mA (or 4 mA depending on configuration), and 1000 represents 10 Volts or 20 mA. Adjust the mathematical block settings so your output falls within 0 to 1000. For example, if your math block outputs 60, you'll see 0.6 V (or 1.2 mA) at the analog output.

How can I apply a mathematical formula like X/100 × (Y-Z) + Z, where X is the analog input (0-100%)? Is there a way to do this directly?

You should first multiply, then divide, and finally add Z. In other words: X/100 × (Y-Z) + Z is equivalent to calculating X × (Y-Z), then dividing by 100, and finally adding Z. What are your actual input signal (analog input), and what do you use for X, Y, and Z?

To perform such formula calculations, use the "Arithmetic Instructions" function block. As mentioned before: internally, the controller uses floating-point numbers, but results and parameter entries must be fixed-point values only.

Hello everyone, During my tests with the block "stop watchwatch" of the [product_name] ([article_no]), I observed the following: - The block's output can range from 0 to 65636 for each permitted time unit. The documentation and online help do not mention this. - The "time base" parameter can be set using a text message, but its usefulness is limited since the entry only allows seven characters, making it hard to clearly represent value and unit. Also, when "10 msec" is selected, the unit shown as "msec" does not match the actual output value (which isn't true milliseconds). - For presenting output values, having an optional date format such as hh:mm:ss.xx0 would greatly help. - The block's internal time base for "s", "m", and "h" units is not 0.01s but somewhat less, which means that activating blocks with input pin "En" in parallel, especially with frequent ON/OFF switching, produces inconsistent end-time values. Please refer to the attached circuits: - Test_Stopuhr_01 ([article_no]).lsc: Demonstrates how, using a trick with the "switching delay" block, a value display can be achieved through two units. Particularly, with the 10 ms setting, only durations up to 32 seconds can be shown. This is because the "Ta" parameter in the "switching delay" block requires value input in ms, but the allowed solution is only 10 ms, and the referred value's unit is simply cut off without rounding. From what I understand, adding a WISE-4010/LAN to the [product_name] controller could allow for higher resolution on the analog input. My goal is to connect a 10 kg load cell and read 10,000 units (representing 10,000 grams). Will the [product_name] controller be able to read 10,000 units from the load cell via the WISE-4010/LAN? Also, do I need a separate load cell amplifier or can the load cell be connected directly to the WISE-4010/LAN? Thank you.

The analog inputs of the WISE-4010/LAN offer 12-bit resolution, meaning 4096 units. When measuring 10,000g, each unit will represent approximately 2.44g (10,000g / 4096 units). The analog inputs work with 0/4-20 mA signals, but load cells typically output only millivolts. You’ll need a load cell amplifier that outputs 0-20 mA or 4-20 mA.

If you’re using just a load cell, consider amplifiers with Modbus TCP capability. This often increases the resolution to 16 bits and enables two-way communication, so you can do more than just read the weight.

You mentioned the ADAM-6717 I/O Module. I found a similar module, ADAM-6017, with a good price. It supports Modbus/TCP, provides 16-bit resolution, and includes 8 analog inputs. [url] Is this module compatible for transferring load cell data to the [product_name] controller at higher resolution? I’ve already obtained an amplifier. Kind regards, [user_name]

The ADAM-6717 module can handle small voltage signals and should be suitable for your application. However, you’ll still require a special load cell amplifier since load cells cannot be connected directly to standard analog inputs.

Regarding your note about having the amplifier: Do you now have load cells equipped with the appropriate amplifier? Please specify what kind of signal you’re getting depending on the weight. The ADAM-6017 can communicate with [product_name] controllers, but pay attention to the range of integer values supported. These controllers typically handle integer values from -32,768 to 32,767 (15 bits plus sign) for arithmetic or comparison blocks. Floating point (32 or 64 bit) is available for display, but conversion to 15-bit integer can lose accuracy. If the ADAM-6017 outputs 16 bits without sign (0 to 65,535), values above 32,767 are recognized as negative numbers by the controller. This can be addressed via software blocks, or you can ensure your values remain below 32,767, depending on your application. Regards, [user_name]

I chose the PEPPERL+FUCHS KFD2-WAC2-1.D amplifier based on forum recommendations. I need 10,000 values, aiming for a 1 gram resolution on a 10 kg load cell. From what I’ve learned, the ADAM-6017 should be up to the task. Thanks for the detailed information. Kind regards, [user_name]

The setup should work: connect the load cell to the input of the KFD amplifier, then the amplifier’s analog output to the analog input of the ADAM-6017, and finally, use a patch cable to link the ADAM-6017 to the [product_name] controller. For best results, configure the KFD for 4–20 mA analog output and the ADAM-6017 for 4–20 mA input. The ADAM-6017 can output data as either 16-bit integer or 4-byte float, both readable by the [product_name] controller. With proper scaling, you can achieve a range of 0 to 10,000 for 0 to 10 kg. One point of consideration: investing over 400 euros in components to connect to a controller costing about 100 euros may not be cost-effective if you only need basic weight display; ready-made weight systems might be more economical. Regards, [user_name]

Within the [product_name] [version_no] app bundle, there’s an info.plist file where users can change the jre_path key to force Java 8 usage, rather than AWS Corretto 11. Debugging by directly opening the Mach-O binary can expose hidden errors that don’t appear when launching from Finder. By default, [company_name] leaves the jre_path empty, so the system/global JRE is used, determined by /usr/libexec/java_home. Installing another JRE later may render the app unusable. Some developers bundle the JRE with the application to avoid conflicts; this isolates the Java environment. It's tricky when Java bytecode and JRE versions don’t match, or with Python if dependencies break on version changes.

Here’s a user-friendly method for managing Java on macOS: Java runtimes are stored in /Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines, and /usr/libexec/java_home helps select among installed runtimes. [product_name] [version_no] requires Java 11, while the InstallAnywhere installer needs Java 8. Both must be x86_64 binaries. In Terminal, after extracting Setup.app, run: export JAVA_VERSION=1.8; open Setup.app. This sets the environment for Java 8 during install, switching to Java 11 for app usage later. The info.plist file JVMVersion key is set to 1.8, but macOS may still use another installed version, so explicit environment setup is needed.

[user_name], I ran some tests and found that the [product_name] PLC does not automatically provide DB1 in OPC Scout, so you must enter the address manually. You have a couple of options: drag “&statepath” to see the syntax and copy it to another line. When you click in the 'ID' column, a button lets you open a dialog to change the 'Item ID/name.' Depending on which PLC address you wish to access, you can enter: S7:[Logo_TCP1]DB1,INT2,1 or S7:[Logo_TCP1]DB1,INT4,1. The PLC always uses DB1 for addressing. 'INT2' maps to DBW2 as an integer, and ',1' means only one element is read (an integer). Another example would be: S7:[Logo_TCP1]DB1,X0.0,1. If you prefer, you can set up symbolic addressing by entering these addresses into the OPC Symbol Editor. Then, within 'Communication Settings -> [product_name] NET configuration -> OPC Settings -> Symbols,' load the symbol file and see your symbolic names in a '\SYM:' folder.

For illustration: If MyUDF1 and MyUDF2 both contain M1, and no markers have been used yet in the program, then adding MyUDF1 first assigns it M1, and adding MyUDF2 next assigns it M2. Second, with the PWM block, you can set a minimum period of 0.01s. That’s why [company_name] doesn’t give exact info about cycle time and switching rate for transistor outputs.

According to the manual, the transistor outputs support: Ohmic load: 10 Hz Inductive load: 0.5 Hz. I've seen higher values on standalone modules but those are not guaranteed and depend on many factors. Operation in the kHz range isn't achievable.

The manual also notes that the maximum switching rate is determined solely by the program cycle time.

Hi, in practical use, the maximum frequency depends on the cycle time of the [product_name], but this cycle time isn't constant. It's affected by using extra features, such as I/O status, web server, access tools, data logging, online tests, and communication with HMI, Modbus, PLC, etc. In some PLCs, timer interrupts can help manage this, but [product_name] lacks programmable interrupts. The numbers—10Hz and 0.5Hz—are more typical for these circumstances.

If you want to know how fast the actuator behind the transistor output can switch, the cycle time isn’t too important, since it's often much smaller than 100ms/2000ms. If the module’s output pin is used internally in the [product_name] program diagram, then only the cycle time matters—here, the output pin works like a flag. There’s a section in the manual (chapter B) on measuring cycle times, and it’s already established here that cycle time is not constant.

Attached are screenshots from tests with a [product_name] module. They show the test program, the simple web server, and the extended web server. The measured cycle frequency is about 25 Hz higher without the simple web server enabled. These cycle frequencies also fluctuate.

You intend to send the analog signal to an external display for visibility. What type of signal does the display require—0-10V or 4-20mA? I’ve attached an example demonstrating both methods. For instance, analog inputs from pressure sensors measuring 0-6 bar could route to one analog output (0-10V), while sensors measuring 0-12 bar could route to another output (4-20mA). Digital inputs allow you to select which sensor value is sent to the output. The recommended process: (1) scale the analog inputs, (2) assign them to an analog multiplexer, (3) use an input to select the desired pressure value, (4) scale for the analog output. The output always needs a value from 0-1000 steps, so if your sensor reads up to 1200 steps, the conversion factor is 1000/1200 = 0.83. Configure analog amplifiers using this gain factor. If sensors have varying ranges, you’ll need more multiplexers and amplifiers to handle the scaling. Also see this FAQ: [document]. For handling more than eight sensors, using an external multiplexer or a higher-capacity CPU might be necessary.

Hello, I am seeking clarification on the difference between [product_name] and [product_name] Slave in a network project. My understanding is that the [product_name] slave does not necessarily need its own program, although it can have one. Is there any additional information about this? The key distinction is that a [product_name] slave operates without a user program, whereas a [product_name] master utilizes the I/O of the slave. Masters can exchange data using S7 communication, allowing you to configure one [product_name] (master) as clients and the others as servers. In your setup, you could create three S7 client connections on one device, and assign the other three devices as S7 servers. In this arrangement, all four [product_name] devices are considered 'masters.'

There are two types of communication for [product_name] S7 connections: 1) Master/slave communication, where one device is set as master and the other as slave, with the slave not running its own program and providing hardware resources to the master; and 2) Client/server connections, where one device is the client and the other the server—here, both devices have their own programs. The client determines what data is sent or received, and device roles are defined during connection setup. There are several methods available to create such connections.

The issue arises because [product_name] only operates with integers in the range of -32,768 to 32,767; any decimal points are purely for display. Gains can be set with two decimal places, but this is just for visual presentation. Internally, the values are handled as integers multiplied by 100 (e.g., a gain of 1.00 equals 100). If you set a gain of 0.1 followed by 2.25, the intended output is 0.225, but in [product_name], the calculation is 10/100 * 225/100 = 0.225. Due to integer rounding, this becomes 0.23, meaning the actual total gain is 0.23. Such rounding introduces noticeable value jumps with small gains. As an alternative, consider using a single gain of 2.25 and displaying one decimal place. You can compare the results using the example provided.

In the second example, the amplification factor is multiplied by ten. With the first method, after analog amplification, you get output values between -40 and 140, which are shown as such. With the second method, you receive values from -400 to 1400, corresponding to a displayed range of -40.0 to 140.0 if you display a decimal place in the analog amplifier. Backlight flags: Flags M25, M28, and M29 are used to control the backlight of the onboard display. Flags M26, M30, and M31 manage the backlight for the [product_name] operator device. The outputs from timers, message texts, or other function blocks can be used to activate the backlight flags. If you use markers M25, M28, or M29 within the logic, automatic backlighting for the onboard display via cursor keys will be disabled. Similarly, using M26, M30, or M31 means the operator device's backlighting won't switch on automatically via button presses. Refer to the provided attachment for further details.

How are the bits in the shift register set to 1? You can also create output sequences, like for lights in a supercar. Thanks.

The state present at the input of the shift register is transferred when the trigger transitions from low to high. Hello, I am having trouble determining the correct gain and offset values for a 4-20mA sensor input. For example: 100 °C corresponds to 20mA and reads as 1000 units on the [product_name], while 0 °C relates to 4mA and the result is unclear on the [product_name]. The increment is 50, with an offset of -250 and a gain of 1.25, which seems confusing. I am unsure why the offset is not 200. While I can generally calculate gain and offset, the 4-20mA setup is causing issues. Could someone explain how to calculate gain and offset in this scenario?

The analog input on [product_name] typically interprets a 0-20 mA current signal (or 0-10V voltage) and translates it to 1000 units. For a 4-20 mA sensor, 4 mA serves as the zero point, leaving 800 usable units from 200 to 1000. Therefore, both amplification (gain) and zero-point adjustment (offset) are required. If you amplify the 1000 units with a gain of 1.25, this becomes 1250 units. Applying an offset of -250 shifts the measurement range from -250 to 1000.

Thank you, your explanation is accurate and very helpful. If we want to convert a 4-20mA signal to display 0-1000 units on [product_name], we should set the gain to 1.25 and the offset to -250. However, I would like to know if there is a formula for calculating these values myself for 4-20mA sensors. One formula could be: gain = (max sensor value - min sensor value) / (max normalized value – min normalized value). For example: gain = (20 - 4) / (1000 - 200) = 0.02. Offset = [(min sensor value x max normalized value) – (max sensor value x min normalized value)] / (max normalized value – min normalized value), so offset = [(4 x 1000) - (20 x 200)] / (1000 - 200). Best regards, [user_name]

When setting up a 4-20 mA sensor in the analog amplifier, manual calculations are unnecessary as the [product_name] software computes these automatically. You simply select the 4-20 mA sensor type, input minimum and maximum limit values for the measured range, and specify decimal places. The software then determines the gain and offset for you. For example, with a 4-20 mA sensor ranging from -30 bar to 90 bar and one decimal place: Type: 4-20 mA, Minimum: -300, Maximum: 900. The software calculates a gain of 1.5 and an offset of -600.

Thank you for your reply. I am aware that [product_name] calculates gain and offset automatically and that it's sufficient to input only the minimum and maximum values. Based on your example—gain = 1.5 and offset = -600—I'd like to understand how to manually calculate these for a 4-20mA sensor. Is there a standard method, or does [product_name] use a specific approach for 4-20mA signal conversion? Best regards, [user_name]

It is possible to manually compute the gain and offset values. For example, a sensor with 4-20 mA range and a measurement scale from -30 to 90 bar (displayed with one decimal). If you want -30 bar to correspond to 4 mA, you would need to extend the measuring range as it would typically be set for a 0-20 mA sensor.

When the [product_name] device is powered on or restarted, all VM memory values reset to 0 because the VM memory isn't retained.

That's the default behavior. What I'm aiming for is to have the value set to 1 upon startup. There's a startup signal called M8. Is it possible to use this somehow? The manual notes: "The M8 flag is set during the first cycle after startup and can be used in your logic diagrams for initialization."

Unfortunately, that's not doable. You can't assign specific states (0 or 1) to network inputs directly in the [product_name] logic diagram.

It's a bit more complicated, but I've encountered a similar issue before (network input state retrieval is delayed after device startup). A simpler workaround is to read the network input using a delay block—for example, only accept the input's state change if it remains True for two seconds. For analog inputs and variable memory, one method involves using an analog multiplexer: feed the network analog input through an amplifier, and route its output to one multiplexer input. Assign a default value through another amplifier offset to the multiplexer’s second input. Link the multiplexer output to the network output at the VM address (like VW10). A better method is to use Parameter VM Mapping, assigning the multiplexer output to the address directly. You now have a choice between input or default value based on how the multiplexer is switched (using M8 flag with a delay trigger after startup). After a few seconds, switch the multiplexer back to the network input once the connection is restored. To further improve, you can retain the previous analog input value using a functional block with retention, so the last value is stored and restored on power-up.

No, you shouldn't connect multiple outputs to a single input—it's not the proper approach. Instead, use an OR gate. Since the device version isn't specified, I can't give a detailed diagram, but here's an idea: Connect network input to one side of the OR gate; link an off-delay block triggered by the M8 flag to the other side of the OR gate; wire the off-delay reset to the network input. Set the off-delay block for a few seconds (enough time for network synchronization). If the network input goes high before the timer runs out, it resets and won't interfere further. This lets you manage just one network input (though using an RS trigger with two network inputs is also an option).

However, there are a few things to watch out for. When calling a UDF in your program, the block numbers for those within the UDF will be automatically assigned to available numbers, which also applies to flags. For example, if your UDF contains 13 blocks and 2 flags, calling it five times will use 65 blocks and 10 flags.

There isn't a reference function 'hh:mm' available, as seen in the manual under 'Editing a parameter box.' The reference is a single integer. For 04:30 (hh:mm), that's 4 * 60 + 30 = 270 minutes; no separate entry for hours and minutes. Only in unreferenced timers can you enter hours and minutes into separate fields. So: Parameter Hours hh:mm is the same as reference minutes. Parameter Minutes mm:ss is the same as reference seconds. Parameter Seconds ss:1/100s is the same as reference ten milliseconds. Hi, Here’s more context related to [user_name]'s solution: The approach is correct since [product_name] does not have a timing block that can be paused using an external signal. The only option is to create a custom timer using a pulse generator and counter(s), similar to [user_name]'s suggestion. To minimize timing errors (especially if the pause signal frequency is high), set TH = TL and keep TH + TL small. You’ll also need a sufficiently high [product_name] cycle frequency. In some cases, it may help to add a pre-divider between the pulse generator and main counter (constructed with a counter and a marker at the counter output, and a signal line to the CLR pin of this counter—ON = OFF sets the pre-divider value). With this, you can achieve a time base of 0.05 s + 0.05 s = 0.1 s and use a secondary counter for full seconds. See also similar questions: "Can I pause timers or programs". Best regards, [user_name]

I'm not entirely sure what you want to achieve. With the threshold set to switch ON at -120 and OFF at -119, the trigger acts exactly as configured. Are you aiming for the trigger to turn ON at -120 and for lower values, then OFF again at -119? If so, set the ON threshold to -200. Then, the trigger will stay ON for values from -200 to -120.

Thanks, that suggestion worked. Setting ON to -200 and OFF to -120, every time I slide the input from minimum to maximum, the block turns positive and my issue is solved. However, I'm still uncertain why it didn't work when set to ON: -121 and OFF: -120. The block should create a positive signal as I slide the input from max to min, passing the ON point—a brief pulse to activate the latching relay. But this doesn't happen unless I manually change the analog value with small arrow clicks during simulation.

With the ON = -121 and OFF = -120 parameterization, the threshold trigger operates within just one unit. If the real [product_name] amplifies the signal and skips over this narrow range, it may miss the value (-121). The analog-to-digital converter requires time to process the analog signal.

Got it, that makes sense now. Thanks.

Depending on the resolution and rounding in [product_name], after reaching -118, the next value could be -122 or in the opposite direction. Refer to the analog threshold trigger help: there are two ways to use it. If you set both ON and OFF to -120, the trigger activates and stays ON until the value drops back to -120 or below; this works well for your RS block. If the value fluctuates, you need a hysteresis—like ON at -120 and OFF at -130. The difference is the hysteresis: ON => OFF. I usually use an analog differential trigger with ON = my value and Delta = -10; delta serves as hysteresis, so only one setpoint is required. Regards, [user_name]

Suppose the range is 0 - 80°C. If I input 2V and get a value of 202, can I subtract 202 from the analog input to set the zero point? Is it possible to perform such a mathematical adjustment on the analog input?

Here is the screenshot.

Regarding the basics: The A/D converter for an analog input translates 0-10V or 0/4-20mA signals into approximately 1,000 units. If you use a 2-10V (or 4-20mA) input, you only get 800 units, since 200 units for 0-2V (or 0-4mA) are not used. To adjust for this, you need to set the analog amplifier so that a 0-10V (or 4-20mA) signal covers the range, and shift the starting point (OFFSET). For example, 80°C over 800 units results in 0.1°C per unit. At 0.1°C for 1,000 units, you get 100°C. With a measuring range of 80°C, there is an offset of 20°C (200 units). This means the adjusted measurement range stretches from -20°C to 80°C.

Relay outputs always make a slight clicking sound when they switch on or off.

Are there any limits on the number of instances that can be added to [product_name] memory? I'm planning to use a PC-based system to adjust [product_name] program parameters regularly. If I modify the [product_name] program daily, could this cause the system to fail over time?

Hello, I'm not entirely sure what you mean by changing the program daily. If you download a new program every day, [product_name] should have the same restrictions as other controllers that use internal EEPROM. Generally, EEPROM can handle up to 100,000 write cycles. This would mean [product_name] could last for about 274 years if you write once each day. So, the risk of causing damage through daily downloads is extremely low and unlikely to be a concern during typical use. Hope this helps.

Thank you, [user_name]. You addressed my concern. The scenario I'm considering involves setting daily timers to control electronic devices. Hello [user_name], The point about EEPROM is that downloading a new program to [product_name] uses up one write cycle, up to a maximum of 100,000 downloads. However, if you simply change timer parameters through the panel, using the cursor buttons or non-password-protected menus, or edit via message text and the OK button, you are not re-downloading the program, so this doesn't affect memory durability. The device will retain different versions locally and on the PC, but the EEPROM wear occurs only with actual program downloads. If your PC changes parameters in each block and then downloads them daily, that would eventually reach the write cycle limit, but realistically, it would take centuries. A better solution is to use the TD panel along with menu structures described on the official application example site ([url]). With up to 50 pages, you could set a timer for each, independently. Some examples for setting counters and navigating messages are covered on the application example page. You can also set retention for counters and timers, so your settings aren't lost during a power failure. Frequent use may wear out panel buttons, so custom overlays are suggested to protect them and allow personalization of the display. Hope this clarifies! ("Have a great day!")

A digital signal from one module can also receive multiple data sets at the same input via coding. If you need to transfer more complex data or further reduce the number of lines, simple communication protocols such as impulse-count commands or short serial data packets (with or without dedicated clock lines) can be used, though this requires suitable circuitry within all connected [product_name] modules. You cannot write to a physical digital input; you are only able to read the state of a physical digital input.

To change the state of Q1, you can: 1. Remove the connection between I1 and Q1. This allows you to control Q1 directly with C#. It's also possible to directly write to M1-M64, provided the left side of the flag is open. 2. Add an OR block between I1 and Q1, and add a network input NI1 to the OR block. This gives you the ability to change the status of Q1 through either I1 or NI1. For NI1, you can use a local VM address (e.g., V0.0, which is the first bit of the DB block). Usable addresses for bits include V0.0-V0.7, V1.0-V1.7 up to V850.0-V850.7. You can also use bytes (VBx), words (VWx), or double words (VDx) for statuses, counters, or integer values, but be sure not to overlap addresses (if using V0.0, avoid using VB0, VW0, or VD0 at the same time). I'm struggling to understand why my analog input amplifier blocks, with a -10VDC input on my [product_name] device ([version_no] running the latest firmware and using [version_no] [product_name]), are giving mismatched output values in VRW1 and VRW2. For example, when both the input and amplifier block output show 1000 (full scale), I expect the VRWs to also read 1000, but they read 771 and 768 instead. When the input is zero, the output is also close to zero as expected. It seems like some scaling is happening, but I can't identify why. The same logic on AI3 and AI4 works correctly—1000 in, 1000 out; zero in, zero out. Why are the VR stored words apparently getting scaled or changed? Any ideas? Thanks, [user_name] in New Zealand

Your issue is due to an overlap in VRW address allocation. The memory addressing is byte-based rather than word-based and starts at address 0. When using words (2 bytes each), you need a gap of 2 between addresses—for example, VRW0, VRW2, VRW4, and so on. Incorrect allocation causes data overlap, while correct allocation avoids this issue.

Hello, I have a question regarding analog inputs. As known, input I7 in [product_name] [article_no] can be used as an analog input (0-10V). What happens if more than 10V is supplied to that input? For example, if 24V is connected to I7, does [product_name] treat it as if 10V was supplied, or does it behave differently, mapping 0-24V to the internal value range 0-1000? I want to confirm that anything above 10V is interpreted as 10V, with the internal value capped at 0-1000. Also, can I use I7 and AI1 simultaneously in one program? How does [product_name] handle this scenario?

When using I7 as an analog input (0-10V), the maximum value is 10V, equating to an internal value of 1000. If you connect 24V DC, it's necessary to use resistors so that only 10V reaches the input, with any excess voltage dropped across the resistor. Voltages up to 12V DC are generally not problematic (12VDC would still correspond to a 1000 internal value).

Input terminals can function as either analog or digital, depending on your programming. If AI1 (I7) is set in the analog comparator and 24V DC is connected, the value becomes 1000. Both can be used at the same time—see attached example program. If the analog value passes the digital '1' threshold, the digital path activates; below 10V, the analog path works as expected up to 1000. The voltage level for digital '1' activation varies, but the manual provides a reference value. For [product_name] [version_no] units, digital '1' is typically recognized around ~6V DC. Please refer to the documentation for precise details.

Greetings [user_name], [user_name], and [user_name]! The explanations above are correct. It’s possible to use both analog and digital inputs simultaneously in a program, but it's important to be cautious about their interaction. On a [product_name] [version_no], digital inputs are defined as: signal '0' for voltages below 5V, and signal '1' for voltages above 12V (since it's designed for 24V DC digital inputs). Therefore, an analog signal between 0-24V DC will be mapped internally between 0-1000 while the input remains within the 0-10V (possibly up to 12VDC) range. Around 12V DC, the digital input I7 switches to 'high', but this threshold is not exact—you may need to experiment. Note that analog-capable inputs (I1, I2, I7, and I8) have lower current sensitivity and higher impedance (72 kOhm) compared to other digital inputs. On [product_name] [version_no], digital '1' is recognized above 8.5V DC due to expected digital input ranges of 12-24V DC. The analog signal will be processed within 0-10V, corresponding to 0-1000 internally, and remains fixed at 1000 for signals above 10V DC. The digital input switches at about 12V DC on one model or 8.5V DC on another. This dual-use acts as an analog threshold trigger, with threshold values set at 999 or 849 based on your selected sensor type; see the documentation for details. If you connect an analog signal around 5.7V DC (internal value 571) and then change the input to 12V DC or 24V DC using a switch, the digital input will activate, and the analog value will jump to 1000, which may affect your program logic. Use caution!

Did you have difficulty understanding the previous responses? The analog inputs are not compatible with direct 0/4 to 20mA signals.

[article_no] only supports 0-10V for analog inputs (up to four analog channels). If you want to use 0-20mA, 4-20mA, or PT100 signals, you will need additional expansion modules. [url] There are also third-party converters (4-20mA to 0-10V) available.

As mentioned before, using a 500 ohm resistor as a converter works as well.

[url] Here is a practical example: If a 0-10Vdc input is used to measure a 4-20mA signal, Ohm's law applies: R=V/I, where V is voltage and I is current. For 10V and 20mA, the required resistance is 500 ohms. With 20mA through a 500 ohm resistor, there is a 10V drop; with 4mA, it drops 2V. So, a 4-20mA signal across a 500 ohm resistor yields 2-10V. The resistor's tolerance should be 1% or less, preferably 0.1%, to maintain accuracy. Any variation can affect measurement precision. After installing the resistor, check actual readings and adjust your software as necessary. For instance, a 500 ohm resistor might measure 497.5 ohms, resulting in a voltage range of about 1.99 to 9.95V instead of 2 to 10V. Connect the resistor across the voltage input terminals of your data acquisition device, and then connect your 4-20mA signal across the same terminals. As current flows, voltage is created and measured by the system. Ensure you properly ground the power supply if required.

I'm trying to adjust the 'connection time' for a weekly timer through a webserver created with [product_name], but it's not working. Adjustments for other timers are straightforward, but the weekly timer is problematic. When I try to set the 'connection time', it appears as a 4-digit hexadecimal value. Assigning this value to a variable causes it to display in decimal, and when read from the webserver, it's interpreted as minutes using the decimal value. How can I input a value for the 'connection time' of the weekly timer via a webserver set up in [product_name]?

The switching times for the weekly timer are encoded in BCD format. If you transfer the switch-on time as a word to memory, hours are stored in the left byte and minutes in the right byte. For instance, if the switch-on time is at address VW0, the bits V0.4 to V0.7 represent tens of hours, V0.0 to V0.3 represent ones of hours, V1.4 to V1.7 are tens of minutes, and V1.0 to V1.3 are ones of minutes. Therefore, you need to use the hexadecimal format in [product_name]. Create two separate input/output fields for each byte: one for hours and another for minutes. The analog-to-digital converter for these analog inputs converts all signals into a 0-1000 unit scale, whether it's 0-10V, 0/4-20mA, or PT100/1000. I am working with a 2-wire PT100 sensor, connecting it to a [product_name] [article_no] model that runs on 12/24V. What is the correct way to wire it to the controller? The AM 2 PT100 module allows direct connection, but when I connect the PT100 directly to the [product_name] at L+ and I7 or I8—and configure the program sensor to PT100—A1/A2 displays 1000. The closest I have come to a successful setup uses a resistor network as a voltage divider: a 560 ohm resistor from M to I7 and the PT100 from I7 to L+. With this, I read 177 at room temperature. My aim is to operate a solar water heater pump. I found and downloaded a program in another thread, so I’m set on the programming side.

Hello [user_name], a caution for your setup! 1) The PT100 sensor is a resistor with a value of 100 ohms at about 0°C, and its resistance changes in a fairly linear way over the temperature range -50...+200°C (exact values can be found online). 2) The AM2 PT100 module from [company_name] uses a bridge circuit with the PT100 as one leg, so resistance changes have a significant impact on the measured value. 3) This is why PT100 modules allow both 2-wire (less precise) and 3-wire (more precise) connections—the 3-wire option makes it possible to compensate for resistance in the wiring by passing known currents and measuring wire resistance, which then gets subtracted. It's been a long time since I last described this process, so my explanation might be a bit fuzzy. 4) If you connect the PT100 sensor as you described, directly to a 0..10 V analog input on a [product_name] [article_no], together with a resistor voltage divider, you need to be careful when choosing the resistor values, their tolerance (temperature stability), and their power rating (in Watts). 5) Standard 1/2 or 1/4 W carbon resistors typically have a tolerance of 5-10%, meaning their value can shift by 5-10% due to temperature changes. So a 560 ohm resistor might vary by up to ±56 ohms, which could mask the PT100's resistance change that represents the process temperature. It's better to use high-quality resistors (see attached) chosen for their stability. Suppliers like RS-Components carry such items. 6) You can always adjust for value ranges in the [product_name] program; using an excel sheet created by Betel makes it easier to calculate gain and offset, and to design amplifier stages for precise range. 7) One calibration approach is to place the PT100 in an ice slush (close to 0°C), keep all resistors constant, and check the value in [product_name] Soft Comfort. Use this 'zero' point to improve calibration. Hope this helps! Cheers [user_name]

It looks like you have overlapping in your VM addresses. Could you share the Modbus register table for the inverter?

I suspect the problem is with the format. I'm attempting to read as uint16, but I'm unsure how to configure this in [product_name].

Your main issue is with overlapping addresses in VM memory. The addressing is based on bytes, not words—a word consists of two bytes. The address of the word is determined by the left byte. For example: VW0 = VB0 + VB1, VW1 = VB1 + VB2, VW2 = VB2 + VB3. As you can see, VW0 and VW1 both use VB1, VW1 and VW2 both use VB2. To avoid overlap, set the addresses of VWs at intervals of two bytes, like VW0, VW2, VW4, etc. The standard analog network input (NAI) is designed for INT16 values (range -32,768 to 32,767), not for UINT16 (range 0 to 65,535). If the value exceeds 32,767, [product_name] interprets it as a negative number.

Use memory variables (like Vx.y) instead of direct inputs for writing purposes. Outputs can be controlled, but if the output is used in the controller program, its value will be overwritten by the previous logic. Hope this helps.
